subject: general
question: If the length of a uniform metallic conductor is doubled, and simultaneously its area of cross-section is doubled, how does the resistance of the conductor change?

options.text: It remains the same as the original resistance.
It becomes four times the original resistance.
It decreases to one-half of the original resistance.

solution:
The correct answer is __**It remains the same as the original resistance**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
• The **resistance (R)** of a uniform metallic conductor is mathematically expressed by the formula **R = ρ (L / A)**, where **ρ (rho)** represents the **resistivity** of the material, **L** is the **length** of the conductor, and **A** is the **area of cross-section**. 
• According to the question, the **length is doubled**, meaning the new length **L' = 2L**. This factor alone would typically increase the resistance because **resistance is directly proportional to length**. 
• Simultaneously, the **area of cross-section is doubled**, meaning the new area **A' = 2A**. Increasing the area typically decreases the resistance because **resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section**.
